title: Wipe away tears (Isaiah 25:6–8)
hookLine: a feast of rich food for all peoples, and death swallowed up

lines: GRIEF AND A MEAL, SIDE BY SIDE.
A FEAST WHERE DEATH IS SWALLOWED.
cards: After a funeral, there's usually food. A long table in a church hall, casseroles under foil, someone's well-known potato salad, coffee in big urns.
People who haven't seen each other in years stand holding paper plates, and between the tears there's sometimes laughter. Grief and a meal, side by side.
Today Isaiah takes that same table and turns it inside out: a feast where the guest list is everyone on earth, and what gets swallowed up at the end of the meal is death.

teach.b: Here's the menu, in the King James Bible: "a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined." Fat things meant the best food, the richest cuts.
Wine on the lees is wine left to age on its sediment until it's deep and smooth.
It's a banquet, set on God's mountain, for all people, every nation. Then the feast turns. God removes the covering cast over all peoples, the veil spread over all nations.

Some readers hear a burial shroud, the cloth laid over the dead, lifted off the whole human race. And then: "He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces."
Some readers hear an echo of older stories from that region, where death was a swallower with a huge mouth. Here, the swallower gets swallowed. After the victory, God doesn't make a speech.
God goes face to face, wiping tears off cheeks one by one, like a parent after a nightmare. The New Testament picks these words up twice.

teach.h: HE WILL SWALLOW UP DEATH IN VICTORY.
teach.b: Paul quotes the swallowing of death when he writes about the resurrection. And near the very end of the Bible, Revelation says: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes."
Christians hear in this feast a picture of what they hope for. This week's prophets walked us here: Habakkuk's yet, the God who sings, a bag with holes, Zerubbabel, the donkey king, hearts turned.
And now, a table set for everyone.

how: Isaiah 25:6–9 is among the funeral readings in some churches, and some Christians connect its feast with the communion meal and with the hope of resurrection.

o: a tent where pilgrims sleep at a festival
a white robe worn to a wedding feast
a burial cloth laid over the dead

games.q: what's inside Isaiah 25 — tap the pairs.
p: heard by some as a burial shroud
God shall wipe away all tears

s: Isaiah's feast is only for one nation
it's for all people. the veil is lifted from every nation.
Paul quotes Isaiah 25 about the resurrection
he writes that death is swallowed up in victory.
in the passage, God wipes away tears with a speech
God wipes tears from off all faces: close, face by face.

games.q: the feast is over and death has been swallowed up. what does God do next, in Isaiah's picture?
o: wipe the tears from every face.
games.why: "the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces." the victory ends in a close, personal gesture.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've lost, or someone grieving now, and let yourself feel it for a moment; Isaiah's feast doesn't skip the tears.

Then picture a table and who you'd want at it, someone lonely, someone far from home, and picture setting the plate in front of them. If you pray, give thanks for the people at your table; if not, simply hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Shroud, the burial cloth laid over the dead: Isaiah's picture of God lifting it off every nation at a feast where death is swallowed up.

carryVoice: Your line: tears wiped away. Face by face, one by one. Day four hundred ninety-seven, and another week walked.
